title: ESSAY 2: The Rise of Non-Performing Assets in Indian Banks — Causes, Consequences and Cures

blocks.content: (Word Count: ~350 words | Type: Analytical | Level: SBI PO / RBI Grade B / CBO)

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: A loan is classified as a Non-Performing Asset (NPA) when interest or principal installment remains overdue for more than 90 days in standard loans or two crop seasons for short-duration agricultural crops.
Primary causes of rising NPAs include aggressive lending practices, unviable project appraisals, governance failures, policy paralysis, and macroeconomic downturns.
High NPAs give rise to the 'Twin Balance Sheet' problem, constraining bank lending capacity, depressing corporate investment, and slowing overall economic growth.

Major legal and institutional cures include the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC) 2016, Asset Reconstruction Companies (ARCs), National Asset Reconstruction Company Limited (NARCL), and the SARFAESI Act 2002.

blocks.content: Non-Performing Assets reflect not just financial stress on bank balance sheets, but a deeper structural constraint on credit growth and overall macroeconomic stability.

The spectre of Non-Performing Assets (NPAs) — loans where the borrower has failed to service interest or principal for more than 90 days — has haunted India's banking system for over a decade, threatening the stability of the financial system and the government's fiscal resources. At its peak in 2018, the Gross NPA ratio of Indian public sector banks touched a staggering 14.6%, representing approximately Rs. 10.35 lakh crore of stressed assets — a figure that fundamentally challenged the health and credibility of India's banking sector.

The roots of this NPA crisis are multi-layered. The credit boom of 2004–08, fuelled by optimistic growth projections and insufficient due diligence, resulted in aggressive lending to infrastructure and power sectors that subsequently fell victim to regulatory bottlenecks, land acquisition failures, and the reversal of global commodity cycles. The management of many banks — both public and private — prioritised loan growth over credit quality, aided by a governance culture that was reluctant to reject politically or socially influential borrowers. The concept of 'ever-greening' — providing fresh loans to prevent recognition of earlier bad ones — masked the true extent of stress for years. Additionally, the absence of a time-bound insolvency resolution mechanism allowed promoters of insolvent companies to retain control of assets, diluting recovery prospects for creditors.

rows: Total value of all loans defaulted by borrowers in the bank's portfolio
The actual bad asset value remaining after deducting provisions set aside by the bank
Gross NPA = Total Non-Performing Loans / Total Advances
Net NPA = Gross NPA - Provision Coverage Amount
Measures the overall quality of loan origination and risk management
Reflects the actual financial risk and balance sheet burden faced by the bank

blocks.content: The consequences of this NPA crisis were severe. Capital erosion forced the government to inject Rs. 3.10 lakh crore into public sector banks through recapitalisation bonds between 2016 and 2022 — a significant fiscal burden. Credit growth slumped as risk-averse banks tightened lending standards, creating a 'credit crunch' that disproportionately hurt MSMEs and small businesses. The banking system's ability to support economic growth was seriously compromised.

The response has been multi-pronged and has yielded encouraging results. The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC) 2016 created a time-bound creditor-in-control resolution framework that fundamentally altered the negotiating power between banks and defaulting promoters. The SARFAESI Act and the strengthened DRT mechanism expedited secured asset recovery. Asset Reconstruction Companies (ARCs) and the government-backed NARCL ('Bad Bank') provided alternate avenues for NPA resolution. Bank mergers have created scale, reducing per-unit operating costs and enabling stronger credit assessment capabilities.

items: Distinguish between Gross NPA and Net NPA: Net NPA = Gross NPA minus Provisioning.
Understand the Special Mention Account (SMA) classification: SMA-0 (1-30 days overdue), SMA-1 (31-60 days overdue), and SMA-2 (61-90 days overdue).
Focus on key judicial and regulatory mechanisms like the IBC 2016, DRTs (Debt Recovery Tribunals), SARFAESI Act, and RBI's Prompt Corrective Action (PCA) framework.

blocks.content: By March 2024, the Gross NPA ratio of scheduled commercial banks had declined to a historic low of approximately 2.8% — a remarkable turnaround achieved through structural reforms, improved supervision, and disciplined lending. Sustaining this improvement requires vigilance, continued investment in credit culture, and the maintenance of strong provisioning buffers to absorb future shocks.

Examiner's Tip: This essay uses the Problem-Cause-Effect-Solution structure that examiners reward in analytical essays. The specific data points (14.6% peak, Rs.10.35 lakh crore, Rs.3.10 lakh crore recapitalisation, 2.8% by 2024) are impressive and show real depth.
